A user wanted to try SigNoz but was discouraged by the number of services in the docker-compose file. They would have to reconfigure each one for their setup (separate network, behind Traefik, figuring out access) without cloning the full repo just to get the config files.
A user tried installing SigNoz on Windows 10 via Rancher Desktop using the 'other platform' docs. It failed on dependencies on sh/bash, and they asked for Windows-specific instructions.

A user had looked at the docs 3-4 times to work out how to report host-level CPU/memory/disk metrics. They found only application-stack integration guides and said the documentation 'has a huge hole in it' for this basic use case.

A user hesitated to self-host SigNoz as their APM on the same Kubernetes infra as their application. They liked cutting an external dependency and cost, but compared it to hosting your own status page on the same servers as your SaaS.
A commenter said ClickHouse, SigNoz's storage backend, is a great DB but 'still not the best at storing timeseries metrics.'

A commenter questioned SigNoz's claim that stitching Prometheus and Jaeger together is painful, suggesting Promscale (a unified metrics/trace backend) may solve that. They still found SigNoz interesting and were glad it supports OpenTelemetry.

README nitpick: it describes deploying on Kubernetes first in 'getting started' and only later links to the Docker guide. The user suggested an overview showing both options, so people see you don't need a full k8s cluster to start.

A commenter said Kafka and Druid in SigNoz's original architecture are expensive and complicated components for an open-core product meant to save money versus Datadog. They argued this guarantees many people won't use the 'open' part.

Another commenter pushed back on the 'No scaling pains. Ever.' claim for Kafka and Druid, saying from experience they often require significant effort to scale and maintain. They noted much of Datadog's value is integrations such as PagerDuty/Slack.
A commenter disputed SigNoz's claim that no open-source observability product with a custom UI integrating metrics and traces existed, pointing to Grafana's offering.

A user said they saw similar results with a hand-rolled ClickHouse logging setup ('Clickhouse go brrr'). They were glad to see an OSS solution that bundles the rest of the observability stack into ClickHouse.

A critic of SigNoz's logs benchmark noted it should mention where Elasticsearch beat SigNoz: trace_id fetches (137x faster) and fetching the first 100 logs (14x faster). They also said ES was likely run non-optimally (no Kafka in front, untuned JVM, default codec).
A commenter said the SigNoz benchmark severely misunderstood how Grafana Loki should be queried for high-cardinality data, citing a GitHub issue on the benchmark repo.

A former Elastic employee listed misconfigurations in SigNoz's benchmark: Logstash instead of Beats, a 256MB Logstash heap, grok instead of dissect, no index template, and mismatched document counts. They also noted the aggregation queries weren't in the repo, and said they were surprised Elastic did so well.

A commenter noted the benchmark data from SigNoz's flog fork uses random dictionary words, which compress poorly. They called 500GB -> 207GB a worst case and expected real logs to compress much better.

A commenter cautioned that the benchmark clusters were tiny (about 4 machines). They said tuning expertise and the uniform shape of the test data limit how well the results predict performance at large scale with heterogeneous log fields.
A commenter pointed out that the SigNoz repo's 'ee/' directory is under a separate license, asking whether that makes it 'open-core' rather than fully open source.
A user wanted to self-host SigNoz for a small project but said the self-hosting setup has more containers than their whole application.
A small-startup user on Datadog said they are hesitant to stay because of the expense. They like SigNoz's self-hosting option and its OpenTelemetry basis.
